title: OpenAI's Chief Scientist Proposes Common AI Limits Measured by Perplexity
excerpt: Jakub Pachocki wants rival labs to agree a capability stop line — and not cross it until safety monitoring catches up. Altman called the essay the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while.
body:
• OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki has proposed that AI developers adopt common limits on model capability, measured by "perplexity" — how accurately a model predicts the next token — and commit not to cross an agreed threshold until monitoring and safety tools reach concrete milestones.
  • Pachocki disclosed OpenAI's own numbers: GPT-4's log perplexity of about 0.91 coincided with the emergence of chain-of-thought reasoning, and models below 0.8 have shown transformative gains in mathematics and cybersecurity.
  • He warned AI could drive fundamental advances in its own training methods as soon as 2027, potentially outpacing the tools used to understand and monitor model behaviour.
  • CEO Sam Altman endorsed the proposal on X, calling the essay "the most important thing OpenAI has published in awhile." No specific threshold value or start date has been proposed yet — for readers who build on these models, nothing changes today; what to watch is whether rival labs sign on.

The world's leading AI labs should agree on a speed limit — and on a shared speedometer to enforce it. That is the proposal OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki laid out in a blog post on Sunday, detailed by Reuters and India Today: developers would adopt common limits on increasingly powerful models, measured by a metric called perplexity, and commit not to cross them until the industry's ability to understand and monitor AI behaviour catches up.

The mechanism: one yardstick, one stop line

Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token — the basic unit of text data — on average. Lower is better: a lower score means the model's predictions are more accurate, and, in Pachocki's argument, the model is more capable. His case for using it as the industry's yardstick is that ordinary capability benchmarks go stale quickly, saturated by each new generation of models, while perplexity can be tracked consistently through pretraining — the phase in which models learn from huge amounts of data and computing power — and compared across companies.

The limit would work as a stop line rather than a slowdown. Developers would jointly specify a first capability threshold and define, in advance, the monitoring and safety milestones that must be met before anyone crosses it — Pachocki pointed to detection tools more advanced than existing chain-of-thought monitors as the kind of milestone involved. In his words: "I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone."

Why OpenAI published its own numbers

To make the proposal concrete, Pachocki disclosed internal figures companies normally guard. GPT-3.5 posted a log perplexity of roughly 0.99; GPT-4 came in at about 0.91, the point at which, he wrote, the model became good at chain-of-thought reasoning — breaking complex problems into steps — paving the way for today's reasoning models. OpenAI's models have since pushed below 0.8, a crossing he associates with transformative capabilities in demanding fields such as mathematics and cybersecurity. He expects the 0.68 to 0.70 range could bring another shift in capability, while stressing it is impossible to say in advance what that shift will be.

"This is the most important thing OpenAI has published in awhile."

— Sam Altman, CEO, OpenAI, on X

Altman amplified the essay on X, saying OpenAI was providing transparency into its pretraining progress and hoping the field could agree to common limits that would "help ensure safety and control." The strategic logic, as India Today summarised it, is to remove the race dynamic: if every major lab is bound by the same stop line, no single company feels pressured to cut corners to keep up.

The warning underneath

The proposal's urgency comes from a timing argument. Pachocki wrote that AI could help drive fundamental advances in AI training methods as soon as 2027 — AI improving the process that improves AI — potentially accelerating capability gains faster than advances in monitoring and safety. He also conceded the metric's limits: training data and evaluation sets differ between companies, making readings hard to compare directly, and perplexity does not capture advances made after pretraining, including chain-of-thought reasoning itself. Building genuinely common standards, he acknowledged, remains a technical challenge.

Pachocki is not the only frontier-lab figure making this argument. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently published a proposal to "pace the frontier," calling on major labs to agree common safety standards — an idea India Today reported drew support from both Altman and Elon Musk — and Anthropic's own IPO filing acknowledged that advanced AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to society." What is still missing is the substance of an agreement: Pachocki did not specify what the first limit should be, when it would take effect, or which labs have committed to anything. Until rivals respond, this is a proposal with a published yardstick and no signatures.
